newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Top S.African general named in apartheid probe.
newsitem.headline: Top S.African general named in apartheid probe.

text.p: South African defence force chief General Georg Meiring is on a list of more than 60 soldiers implicated in apartheid-era dirty tricks including state-sponsored murder, the truth commission said on Thursday.

Truth and Reconciliation Commission deputy chairman Alex Boraine and research head Charles Villa-Vicencio told a news conference that Meiring, appointed by President Nelson Mandela, had been named in a 1992 report commissioned by Mandela's predecessor F.W. de Klerk.

"Clearly this is a very, very serious matter," Boraine said. "It's going to have to be resolved. I think that it will have to involve the minister of defence (Joe Modise) and in particular a discussion with General Meiring where we will put to him certain of the allegations for him to reply to."

The report was prepared by General Pierre Steyn, then military chief of staff, following recurring reports that a shadowy third force of renegade police and army officers were conducting a campaign of violence against black liberation groups.
"The intelligence gathered by General Steyn indicated significant unauthorised and unlawful actions," Boraine said. "More than 60 names of individuals are listed."
No details of the report had been officially disclosed before Thursday and at one time de Klerk, the country's last white president, denied in parliament that it existed in written form.

When Steyn gave the report to de Klerk, he asked three generals on the list -- Meiring, the then defence force chief Kat Liebenberg, and Joffel van der Westhuizen -- to tell him which of those named should be retired early or dismissed.
Acting on their recommendations, de Klerk removed 23 soldiers, including some high-ranking officers, from the force.
"It sounds a strange way to get to the truth," Boraine said of de Klerk's handling of the report.

Asked if de Klerk was suspected of a cover-up, Villa- Vicencio said: "To the extent that he did not initiate a full investigation as recommended by General Steyn, I suppose that conclusion could be reached."

Villa-Vicencio said the Steyn report was based on unsubstantiated intelligence, but added: "It has allegations concerning train violence, assassinations, gun-running through the Kruger National Park, smuggling of ivory, rhino horns etcetera, poisoning, cross-border activities."

In the months and years leading up to South Africa's historic all-race election in April 1994, the political transition was thrown into doubt by frequent mass killings, including apparently senseless attacks on black commuter train passengers.
The commission members quoted Steyn as having told them that some members of the police and defence force had done all they could to hamper his inquiry and had destroyed relevant documents.

Mandela set up the truth commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, with a mandate to investigate human rights abuses on all sides during the apartheid years. The intention is that revealing the full facts will help to reconcile former enemies.

General Liebenberg, now retired, was charged with murder last year in the same trial as former defence minister Magnus Malan. Both were acquitted on charges of being behind a 1987 political massacre in KwaZulu-Natal province.

No substantive charges of human rights abuses have previously been publicly levelled against Meiring. Mandela appointed him as an unsullied general with the loyalty of the white officer corps who would be able to lead his men into integration with their former guerrilla enemies.
